name: Tigrinya
catalog_citation: Kogan, Leonid E. 1997. Tigrinya. In Robert Hetzron (ed.), The Semitic Languages, 424-445. London: Routledge.
catalog_locator: p. 429, section 'Prosody' (saved scanned text layer the copy we, under running head 'TIGRINYA 429'; chapter head '18 Tigrinya / Leonid E. Kogan')
catalog_quote: Stress in Tigrinya has no phonological value and easily shifts from one syllable to another. Dynamic stress is very weak and sometimes almost imperceptible. In many cases it falls on the last syllable, e.g. the euphonic -i: ra' asi 'head', sdbdyti 'woman', Pitch is an important element of the Tigrinya stress pattern, but it is also rather unstable. Dynamic stress and pitch may not coincide: ndbdrd 'to be' (" — high pitch; ~ — dynamic stress). Sentence intonation is clearly predominant over the stress of an individual word, The relationship between these two features requires further investigation, but it is clear that rhythmical units very often do not coincide with single words.
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had
sweep_summary: Tigrinya is not in the catalog. Of the two title-works with stress in the title, Walther 1999 (Deklarative prosodische Morphologie) is prosodic MORPHOLOGY (gemination, reduplication, coalescence, spirantization in Tigrinya verbs) with no stress/accent section — confirmed from the DNB table of contents. the full text is closed. Downing 2010 (Accent in African languages, Survey of Word Accentual Patterns, pp. 381-428, doi 10.1515/9783110198966.1.381) is a secondary continental survey that Glottolog links to Tigrinya; it is paywalled everywhere checked (Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, GUP, BASE/CORE blocked) and StressTyp2 has no Tigrinya entry (0 of 699; No open first-hand stress source beyond those already held by the project from the prior pass was found; The best first-hand statement read is Kogan 1997: 429 (stress non-phonological, weak, mobile, mostly final; pitch and dynamic stress dissociate; sentence intonation dominant), corroborated by Leslau 1941 §26 (Akkele Guzay fieldwork: word accent barely perceptible, pre-geminate syllable more intense, final syllable also accented) and De Vito 1895 (mostly final), while Praetorius 1871 (penult, from Beke/Salt lists) and Schreiber 1887 (initial/antepenult) disagree; Bulakh & Kogan 2013: 267 state prosody has never been systematically studied.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tigrinya has no contrastive or fixed word stress: dynamic stress is weak, unstable and non-phonemic, with a tendency for prominence on the word-final syllable; pitch and dynamic stress can fall on different syllables, and phrase/sentence intonation overrides word-level prominence. Corroborated first-hand by Leslau 1941 §26 p. 15 (Akkele Guzay: 'L'accent du mot est très difficile à noter, car le mot n'a presque pas de relief dans la phrase et son accent s'efface devant l'accent de la phrase. Même dans un mot prononcé isolément le débit est uni.. une syllabe suivie d'une consonne géminée a plus d'intensité.. mais dans ces mots, comme d'ailleurs dans la plupart des mots, la dernière syllabe est également accentuée') and by Bulakh & Kogan 2013 §2.1.2 p. 267 ('Просодия Т.я. систематически не исследовалась.. динамическое ударение выражено слабо и акустически почти неуловимо. Фонологического значения ударение не имеет.' = 'The prosody of Tigrinya has not been systematically investigated.. dynamic stress is weakly expressed and acoustically almost imperceptible. Stress has no phonological value.').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing in Kogan 1997 or Leslau 1941. Only Praetorius 1871 §97 (from Salt's transcriptions) speaks of a 'Nebenaccent' on the final syllable of trisyllables with antepenult main accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Kogan: final-syllable prominence 'in many cases', notably on the euphonic -i; pitch peak and dynamic stress may sit on different syllables (näbärä). Leslau: syllables before a geminate carry extra intensity, final syllable also accented in most words. Nineteenth-century grammars (Praetorius 1871 penult/antepenult with heavy-final attraction; Schreiber 1887 initial in disyllables, antepenult in longer words; De Vito 1895 mostly final in disyllables) give mutually contradictory fixed rules, consistent with the modern 'weak, unstable, non-phonemic' classification.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement, explicitly subordinated to sentence intonation; Kogan notes rhythmical units often do not coincide with single words; Leslau says even citation forms are delivered evenly. Kogan's sketch is of standard (Eritrean/Tigray) Tigrinya generally; Leslau's data are Akkele Guzay (Eritrea).
new_statements.identity_note: Kogan 1997 and Bulakh & Kogan 2013 describe Tigrinya generally (tigr1271, standard Eritrean/Tigray usage). Leslau 1941 describes the Akkele Guzay dialect of Eritrea. Niguss 2021 (silent on stress) describes Rayya Tigrinya (southern Tigray). Praetorius 1871 is based on Aksum/Adwa plus Salt's 'Hauasa' list.

In many cases it falls on the last syllable, e.g. the euphonic -i: rə'asi 'head', säbäyti 'woman'. Pitch is an important element of the Tigrinya stress pattern, but it is also rather unstable. Dynamic stress and pitch may not coincide: näbärä 'to be' (ˊ — high pitch; ˋ — dynamic stress). Sentence intonation is clearly predominant over the stress of an individual word. The relationship between these two features requires further investigation, but it is clear that rhythmical units very often do not coincide with single words.
new_statements.citation: Kogan, Leonid E. 1997. Tigrinya. In Robert Hetzron (ed.), The Semitic Languages, 424-445. London: Routledge.
new_statements.locator: p. 429, section 'Prosody' (scanned page header 'TIGRINYA 429'; scanned renders ä/ə as 'd', normalised here)
new_statements.reading: Tigrinya word stress is non-contrastive, weak and mobile, with a tendency toward the final syllable; pitch prominence and dynamic stress can dissociate, and phrase intonation overrides word-level stress. This is the standard modern reference statement and agrees with Leslau's 1941 first-hand fieldwork (weak word accent, extra intensity before geminates, final syllable also accented) and with De Vito 1895 (mostly final); the older penult/initial/antepenult rules of Praetorius 1871 and Schreiber 1887 rest on missionary or third-party transcriptions. Bulakh & Kogan 2013 add that the prosody has never been systematically studied and that pitch accent claims are unverified. A coding for this language should therefore be 'weak/non-phonological stress, predominantly final, mobile' with low confidence, or 'no fixed word stress'.

sources.quote: Stress in Tigrinya has no phonological value and easily shifts from one syllable to another. Dynamic stress is very weak and sometimes almost imperceptible. In many cases it falls on the last syllable, e.g. the euphonic -i: rəʔsi 'head', säbäyti 'woman'. Pitch is an important element of the Tigrinya stress pattern, but it is also rather unstable. Dynamic stress and pitch may not coincide: näbärä 'to be' (ˊ – high pitch; ` – dynamic stress). Sentence intonation is clearly predominant over the stress of an individual word. sources.note: 'Prosody' (p. 429): stress has no phonological value, shifts easily between syllables, dynamic stress very weak/almost imperceptible; in many cases falls on the last syllable (e.g. euphonic -i); pitch important but unstable and may not coincide with dynamic stress; sentence intonation predominates over word stress.

sources.citation: Leslau, Wolf. 1941. Documents tigrigna (éthiopien septentrional): grammaire et textes (Collection linguistique publiée par la Société de Linguistique de Paris 48). Paris: Klincksieck.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.quote: a) L'accent du mot est très difficile à noter, car le mot n'a presque pas de relief dans la phrase et son accent s'efface devant l'accent de la phrase. Même dans un mot prononcé isolément le débit est uni. b) Une règle générale qui semble se dégager est qu'une syllabe suivie d'une consonne géminée a plus d'intensité qu'une syllabe ayant une consonne simple : sällim « noir », qäddus « saint »; mais dans ces mots, comme d'ailleurs dans la plupart des mots, la dernière syllabe est également accentuée. c) L'informateur du dialecte décrit ici prononce avec gémination une consonne de la syllabe finale accentuée : sällim(m) « noir ».
sources.locator: § 26 Accent (p. 15 per prior index; scanned text, line-break hyphenation joined)
sources.note: §26 Accent (p. 15), Akkele Guzay dialect: word accent very hard to note, the word has almost no relief in the phrase and its accent yields to phrase accent; even in isolation delivery is even; a syllable followed by a geminate has more intensity, but in these as in most words the last syllable is also accented.

sources.citation: Schreiber, J. 1887. Manuel de la langue tigraï, parlée au centre et dans le nord de l'Abyssinie, vol. 1. Vienne: Hoelder.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: 'Accent' (pp. 10-11): affixes unaccented; disyllables regularly accented on the first syllable (unless it has a 6th-order/ə vowel and the second does not); words of 3+ syllables most often antepenult; later notes say accent is 'un peu incertain' in several forms.

sources.note: Second-hand: Tigrinya stress described as shifting readily, dynamic correlates and pitch not always parallel; quotes Kogan 1997 that sentence intonation predominates over word stress (cites p. 439, but the passage is on p. 429 of the 1997 volume).

sources.quote: The position of stress in Tigrinya has been described as shifting readily from one position to another and is not always marked in parallel by dynamic stress correlates (intensity/duration) and pitch. Kogan (1997: 439) suggests therefore that 'sentence intonation is clearly predominant over the stress of an individual word', resembling descriptions noted above for Amazigh varieties which lack stress.
sources.note: Secondary; summarises Kogan 1997 only (the cited page 439 is a slip; the passage is on p. 429). Adds nothing first-hand.

sources.note: §2.1.2 (p. 267): prosody of Tigrinya has not been systematically studied; dynamic stress is weakly expressed and acoustically almost imperceptible, as in other living Ethiosemitic languages; stress has no phonological value; reports of musical (pitch) accent need verification.

sources.citation: Bulakh, Maria S. & Leonid E. Kogan. 2013. Tigrin'ja jazyk [The Tigrinya language]. In M. S. Bulakh, L. E. Kogan & O. I. Romanova (eds.), Jazyki mira: Semitskie jazyki. Efiosemitskie jazyki, 260-310. Moskva: Academia.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 2.1.2. Просодия Т.я. систематически не исследовалась. Принято считать, что, как и в других живых эфиосемитских языках, динамическое ударение выражено слабо и акустически почти неуловимо. Фонологического значения ударение не имеет. Встречающиеся в литературе указания на наличие в Т.я. музыкального ударения нуждаются в проверке.
sources.note: [EN] The prosody of Tigrinya has not been studied systematically. It is generally held that, as in the other living Ethio-Semitic languages, dynamic stress is weakly expressed and acoustically almost imperceptible. Stress has no phonological value. Claims in the literature of a pitch accent in Tigrinya need verification. — No placement rule given.

sources.citation: De Vito, Lodovico. 1895. Grammatica elementare della lingua tigrigna. Roma.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Nelle parole di due sillabe l'accento tonico cade per lo più sull'ultima, p. es. selèf; ma se questa ha la vocale e, e talvolta i, l'accento retrocede sulla prima, p. es. dènghez, kébdi. Nelle parole con tre o più sillabe, l'accento cade di solito sulla vocale di più chiara pronunzia, e a preferenza sull'ultima se questa abbia una à, una o, od una u, p. es. ymellàles, woridù. — Il posto dell'accento tonico è del resto quasi sempre determinato dalla forma della parola.
sources.note: pp. 10-11: in disyllables tonic accent mostly on the last syllable, retracting to the first if the last has e (sometimes i); in 3+ syllables on the 'clearest' vowel, preferably the last if it has a, o, u; position 'almost always determined by the form of the word' (contradicts Schreiber 1887).

sources.citation: Schreiber, J. 1887. Manuel de la langue tigraï, vol. 1. Vienne: Hölder.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 2° Les mots de deux syllabes ont régulièrement l'accent tonique sur la première, à moins que celle-ci ne soit formée par une lettre du sixième ordre et que la deuxième ne soit d'un autre ordre [...] 3° Les mots de trois syllabes et plus ont le plus souvent l'accent tonique sur l'antipénultième; ainsi gäbärä = il fit, egziabihêr = Dieu, etc.
sources.note: [EN] Affixed particles are unaccented; disyllables regularly stressed on the first syllable unless it has a sixth-order (ə) vowel and the second does not; words of three or more syllables mostly on the antepenult. Missionary grammar, contradicts Leslau/Kogan/De Vito on finality.

sources.quote: Bei der Untersuchung über die Betonung sind wir auf Bk. S. beschränkt, da L. den Tonfall nirgends bezeichnet. Zweisilbige Wörter haben den Ton in der Regel auf der Penultima ausgenommen wenn die letzte Silbe geschlossen ist und einen langen Vokal enthält [...] Im Dialekt von Hauasa hingegen wird die allgemeine Gültigkeit obiger Regel durch zahlreiche Ausnahmen beeinträchtigt indem die ultima mag sie consonantisch oder vokalisch auslauten oft den Ton hat [...] Obige Beobachtungen über die Betonung können dem mangelhaften Material entsprechend nur als sehr unvollkommen gelten; sie beziehen sich zunächst auch nur auf das einzelne Nomen ohne Suffixe.
sources.locator: III. Betonung, § 97 (pp. 136-139 per prior index; scanned lightly corrected)
sources.note: §97 'Betonung' (pp. 136-139), second-hand from Beke's and Salt's accent-marked wordlists: disyllables usually penult unless the final is closed with a long vowel; Hauasa (Salt) dialect often final; trisyllables usually antepenult with secondary accent on the final; author calls the observations 'sehr unvollkommen', isolated nouns only.
